messages.subject: [statnet_help] Feature Request
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

Thanks for the suggestions. We are in the process of adding a lot of
features in preparation for the Workshop at this year's Sunbelt Conference
in Corfu (http://nicomedia.math.upatras.gr/conf/Sunbelt2007).

These are good ideas and we have updated "statnet" to version 1.0-14 to
accommodate them. Explicitly:

1) To force the use of the MCMC algorithm for dyad independence models, give
the option "force.mcmc" e.g.,

fit <- ergm(flomarriage ~ edges, algorithm.control=list(force.mcmc=T))

2) There is a new summary command called "Summary.ergm" that returns all the
objects it prints. For example,

# The usual summary
Summary.ergm(fit)
# Save the results
out <- Summary.ergm(fit)
names(out)
out$aic
out$asycov

out

This will be made the default is an upcoming version.

To get the new version, as usual, enter:

library(updatestatnet)

Mark

-------------------------------------------------
Mark S. Handcock
Professor of Statistics
Department of Statistics, C014-B Padelford Hall
University of Washington, Box 354322     Phone:  (206) 221-6930
Seattle, WA  98195-4322.                 FAX:    (360) 365-6324
Web:  www.stat.washington.edu/~handcock
internet:  handcock@stat.washington.edu

messages.subject: [statnet_help] importing edgelist with multiple attributes
messages.body_plain:
Hi Denis,

This is a canonical question. Let's consider your example.
If the file is saved from Excel as a CSV file, R can read it in and
"statnet" can create the network. Explicitly,

> # read in the Excel file saved as a CSV
> x <- read.csv("example1.csv",header=T)
> x
  nodeID1 nodeID2 edgeAttribute1 edgeAttribute2 edgeAttribute3
1       1       2            2.5            566              1
2       1       3            5.2            548              0
3       2       4           10.0            250              0
4       3       4           58.0            365              1
> # Load statnet (network is all that is required)
> library(statnet)
Loading required package: network
...
Type help(package="statnet") to get started.
To cite, see citation("statnet")
> # Create the network fron the edgelist
> g <- network(x[,1:2])
> # Sequentially add each of the edge values
> for(i in 3:5){
+  set.edge.value(g,colnames(x)[i],x[,i])
+ }
> # List them 
> list.edge.attributes(g)
[1] "edgeAttribute1" "edgeAttribute2" "edgeAttribute3" "na"
> # Print out some examples
> as.sociomatrix(g)
  1 2 3 4
1 0 1 1 0
2 0 0 0 1
3 0 0 0 1
4 0 0 0 0
> as.sociomatrix(g, "edgeAttribute2")
  1   2   3   4
1 0 566 566   0
2 0   0   0 548
3 0   0   0 250
4 0   0   0   0
> 

I have attached the example file so you and others can reconstruct it.

This help for the "network" function in Carter Butt's excellent "network"
package has a lot of details in it!

Regards,

Mark

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] two yes/no questions on ERGM in R (fwd)
messages.body_plain:
> 1. My network is very large and I heard that ERGM is computation- 
> intensive.
> Is ERG modeling in R feasible for networks of 1000x1000 or larger?

I can't speak to Statnet in specific, but 1000*1000 may or may not be  
large depending on what you are trying to do. If the goal is a  
statistical analysis in R, it is not too large although one should be  
aware of the way R uses memory. If you're trying to plot such a  
thing, or use certain forms of analysis, then you need to be even  
more careful.

Things to be alert to are:

(1) R uses approximately 8 bytes per cell of a numeric matrix, not  
counting any row and column labels and/or other descriptive vectors  
(partitions from cluster analyses, etc.) This means that the 1k*1K  
matrix you describe consumes 8MB of memory. So this is not at all a  
problem on modern machines.

(2) Data objects that R works with must be entirely in memory. Most  
systems will use some form of virtual memory (on disk) if you exceed  
the available physical memory, but when your computer starts swapping  
R objects in and out of memory, things start to really bog down.  
Treat the available physical memory as an upper limit on what you  
should use.

(3) Many operations in R require copying an entire object. For  
example, changing the value of a cell in a matrix by assignment (e.g.  
m[96,42] <- 7) requires copying the entire matrix. If you do this in  
a loop for several elements, that's one entire copy of the matrix for  
each assignment. This is costly both in space and time. In loops, the  
issue generally is time. Use R's vectorized computations (including  
assignment) to advantage if at all possible, to minimize this  
problem. Other times the issue is (or rapidly becomes) space. For  
example if you conduct a cluster analysis of your matrix, you may  
have a distance matrix that you compute and want to save. This will  
be true for each version of distance you use and want to keep for  
later. If these objects are saved in your .RData file, then they all  
must live in memory together at the same time. This becomes an issue  
as you iterate through solutions to a problem.

(4) Some R functions do very bad things when it comes to memory  
usage, at least when large data sets are being used. For example, glm 
() and lm() create entire copies of your data that are obligatorily  
saved into an object that is returned. Since you often need to save  
these for future use, you may be saving multiple copies of the data  
unnecessarily. I don't know if the ergm package does this, but I  
wouldn't be surprised if it does as this is something of an R  
convention. Also, analyses can create very large data objects that  
are not copies of the data, and these can also get out of control.

(5) Plotting can be very inefficient in R, depending on the package  
used. Again, there are data copying issues (a copy is made to  
represent in the output device), but I know less of the specifics  
here, just that certain reasonable things can work out pretty badly  
if care is not exercised. For example, plotting an hclust object with  
1000 leaves can be reasonably fast, but the same analysis cast as a  
dendrogram object plots exceedingly slowly. I believe this is because  
of the hierarchically structured representation of the dendrogram  
object, as opposed to hclust, which is flatter (for the exact same  
information). Since ergm/statnet/network packages adopt a structured  
representation of their data object, there may be similar performance  
problems, but I wouldn't know for sure.

Some general guidelines of use would be, (i) use a utility such as  
Activity monitor (mac) or top (unix) to keep an eye on the memory  
usage as you work, (ii) force garbage collection if you need to with  
gc(), though keep in mind this may not always free up memory, and  
(iii) save out objects that you are not immediately working with to  
separate RData files. If you don't do these, in the worst case you  
can hang your system. Most OS's will allow you to kill the offending  
process if you get stuck (R), but doing so loses your changes in the  
data since your last save as well as your command history, so do  
everything to avoid this and you will be happier.

If you have a system with, say, 2 GB of ram (reasonably standard  
these days) then for 1M cell matrices you probably will not run into  
too many problems with memory within R, would be my guess. At the  
same time, someone from the statnet team should comment on the memory  
use and time complexity of statnet-specific functions.

Hope this helps,

John Paolillo
Informatics, Indiana University

messages.body_plain:
Martina Morris wrote:
> 
> ---------- Forwarded message ----------
> Date: Sun, 24 Dec 2006 20:37:30 -0800
> From: Denis Trapido <dtrapido@stanford.edu>
> To: morrism@u.washington.edu
> Subject: two yes/no questions on ERGM in R
> 
...
> 1. My network is very large and I heard that ERGM is computation-intensive.
> Is ERG modeling in R feasible for networks of 1000x1000 or larger?

Depends on the terms you employ.  Some of the AddHealth networks are 
larger than that, and I've also run models on some large 
interorganizational interaction networks.  The main issues are:

   1. Making sure you pick terms whose changescores scale well.  Most 
which are in current use are constant or linear time, but this isn't the 
case for all terms (e.g., cycles).

   2. Making sure that the number of parameters and statistics remains 
constrained.  Optimization on 1000+ fixed effects is not pleasant; nor 
are computations for curved models with 1000+ statistics going to scale 
well (unless the way those calculations are internally performed has 
changed recently).

Otherwise, ergm should work just fine -- especially if the graph is sparse.

> 
> 2. Does ERGM in R enable correcting for underselection of non-existing ties
> in the way rare event logit (relogit) does it in Stata?
> 

I don't see that this would be relevant here, but Mark or Dave might 
have other ideas.  (BTW, these are not logit models, except in the case 
of independent dyads.  Or, if you like, the whole thing is a huge 
multinomial logit with one observation, but that's another matter...)

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
John Paolillo wrote:
> (1) R uses approximately 8 bytes per cell of a numeric matrix, not 
> counting any row and column labels and/or other descriptive vectors 
> (partitions from cluster analyses, etc.) This means that the 1k*1K 
> matrix you describe consumes 8MB of memory. So this is not at all a 
> problem on modern machines.

This is true.  Also, note that network objects are stored as edge lists 
(with some indexing and other mojo), so sparse graph storage will not 
scale quadratically in the number of vertices.  (There's some overhead, 
but it's linear.)  Whether this is honored by the various statnet 
routines varies: ergm keeps the network in edgelist form (although some 
term initialization routines might not), but current sna routines 
convert network objects to matrix form prior to analysis.  Such are the 
joys of legacy code.

> 
> (2) Data objects that R works with must be entirely in memory. Most 
> systems will use some form of virtual memory (on disk) if you exceed the 
> available physical memory, but when your computer starts swapping R 
> objects in and out of memory, things start to really bog down. Treat the 
> available physical memory as an upper limit on what you should use.

Also, be aware that the Windows implementation of R seems to have some 
low ceilings on memory allocation.  Those of us in the Linux world 
remain happily immune to this, but we hear of it from our students....

> 
> (3) Many operations in R require copying an entire object. For example, 
> changing the value of a cell in a matrix by assignment (e.g. m[96,42] <- 
> 7) requires copying the entire matrix.

Not always true -- this depends on how the appropriate assignment method 
  is written.  IIRC, most of the standard data types support in-place 
modification, so long as the dimensions of the object are not changed. 
This is also true of network objects, which are almost always modified 
in place.

> If you do this in a loop for 
> several elements, that's one entire copy of the matrix for each 
> assignment. This is costly both in space and time. In loops, the issue 
> generally is time. Use R's vectorized computations (including 
> assignment) to advantage if at all possible, to minimize this problem. 
> Other times the issue is (or rapidly becomes) space. For example if you 
> conduct a cluster analysis of your matrix, you may have a distance 
> matrix that you compute and want to save. This will be true for each 
> version of distance you use and want to keep for later. If these objects 
> are saved in your .RData file, then they all must live in memory 
> together at the same time. This becomes an issue as you iterate through 
> solutions to a problem.

Again, this varies -- R's garbage collection system recaptures most of 
this memory, and many assignments are implemented without copying. 
Because of this, loops are not always faster than the *apply methods, 
despite folk wisdom to the contrary.  However, you are right that R's 
loops are generally pretty slow, and are in some cases space 
inefficient.  Backending can often accelerate highly iterative 
calculations, especially those which would require a lot of object 
handling if performed in the interpreted code.  (My sense, however, is 
that the latter is the real culprit in most of these cases -- working 
with the .Call interface for a while gives one a sense of the vast 
amount of overhead which is involved in supporting R's friendly, 
object-oriented interface.)

> 
> (4) Some R functions do very bad things when it comes to memory usage, 
> at least when large data sets are being used. For example, glm() and 
> lm() create entire copies of your data that are obligatorily saved into 
> an object that is returned. Since you often need to save these for 
> future use, you may be saving multiple copies of the data unnecessarily. 
> I don't know if the ergm package does this, but I wouldn't be surprised 
> if it does as this is something of an R convention. Also, analyses can 
> create very large data objects that are not copies of the data, and 
> these can also get out of control.

This is a very common trope -- it allows secondary methods to perform 
"smart" diagnostics on analysis objects, but does consume a lot of 
memory in some cases.  Similarly, most high-level analysis routines 
perform a number of handy subsidiary calculations which are useful for 
end users, but which consume processor time.  If you are dealing in huge 
data sets, or if you simply need to repeat a specific calculation many 
times (e.g., as do the netlm qap tests), then you should avoid using the 
high-level routines.  Instead, you should employ a function which is 
more appropriately tailored to your particular time/space constraints -- 
most of these routines have back-end components which can be used for 
this purpose.

> 
> (5) Plotting can be very inefficient in R, depending on the package 
> used. Again, there are data copying issues (a copy is made to represent 
> in the output device), but I know less of the specifics here, just that 
> certain reasonable things can work out pretty badly if care is not 
> exercised. For example, plotting an hclust object with 1000 leaves can 
> be reasonably fast, but the same analysis cast as a dendrogram object 
> plots exceedingly slowly. I believe this is because of the 
> hierarchically structured representation of the dendrogram object, as 
> opposed to hclust, which is flatter (for the exact same information). 
> Since ergm/statnet/network packages adopt a structured representation of 
> their data object, there may be similar performance problems, but I 
> wouldn't know for sure.

Well, plot.network (which is a clone of gplot) still coerces its input 
to matrix form for certain purposes, so you'll take a hit there; that's 
rarely a major constraint, however.  IIRC, a bigger issue is the 
overhead involved in creating the polygons to represent the 
edges/vertices, and in having R print them.  I don't worry about this 
too much, however -- by the time this becomes a problem, one's network 
has usually become too large to visualize without more exotic methods 
(especially on a low-resolution display).  A sparse 1000 node network 
should be no problem, in any event.

> 
> Some general guidelines of use would be, (i) use a utility such as 
> Activity monitor (mac) or top (unix) to keep an eye on the memory usage 
> as you work, (ii) force garbage collection if you need to with gc(), 
> though keep in mind this may not always free up memory, and (iii) save 
> out objects that you are not immediately working with to separate RData 
> files. If you don't do these, in the worst case you can hang your 
> system. Most OS's will allow you to kill the offending process if you 
> get stuck (R), but doing so loses your changes in the data since your 
> last save as well as your command history, so do everything to avoid 
> this and you will be happier.
> 
> If you have a system with, say, 2 GB of ram (reasonably standard these 
> days) then for 1M cell matrices you probably will not run into too many 
> problems with memory within R, would be my guess. At the same time, 
> someone from the statnet team should comment on the memory use and time 
> complexity of statnet-specific functions.

FWIW, I don't think that memory is going to be a major constraint for 
most operations on a 1k network (with certain exceptions, such as 1000+ 
parameter models).  I've run diffusion models in R on sparse networks of 
over 100,000 nodes on an Athlon w/2GB of RAM, and nothing was in 
imminent danger of crashing.  Of course, many functions would not be 
feasible on such a network....common sense applies, and YMMV.  The 
statnet library has to balance the disparate demands of versatility, 
performance, and ease-of-use, and users whose requirements push very 
hard on the performance end may find it worthwhile to code something 
more narrowly focused on their specific application.  Of course, no 
software on earth is going to change the fact that many interesting 
network analytic calculations are intrinsically expensive, and you may 
not have enough Time*Iron to get the answer you desire.  Still, 
optimization can sometimes have benefits, if done properly.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

I am having troubles to import valued networks into R.
I have tried both importing data as sociomatrices using this set of commands
loc_density<-read.table("differenceloc_density.txt")
loc_density.dat<-as.matrix(loc_density)
loc_density.net<-as.network(loc_density.dat,loops=T, directected=F)
and importing data as edgelist.loc_density<-read.table("differenceloc_density_edgelist.txt")
loc_density.net<-as.network(loc_density.dat,loops=T, directected=F)
 
I do not get error messages but somehow the value of the network is transformed into binary data.
Do you need to specify somewhere in the as.network command that the network is a valued networks with real number?
 
If I try to get the summary stats for the network I get this error message:
 
Error: protect(): protection stack overflow
 
My memory settings for R are:
max-ppsize=20000  --max-mem-size= 1032662928
 
Can someone help?
 
Thanks in advanced for your time
 
Regards
